5.1 Deconvolution with reference distributions: a review of methods that use more than the mean

Bastien Chassagnol

24 Nov 2026

Source: vignettes/05-1-review-distribution-aware.qmd

Scope

First-generation deconvolution fits a bulk profile with the mean expression of each purified population. This review covers the methods that also use the distribution of the purified profiles: at least their variance, and in some cases a covariance between genes or between cell types. DeCovarT belongs to that family: it plugs in a gene–gene covariance per cell type and maximises a Gaussian-convolution likelihood (population generative vignette).

Every method is read through the same lens: what its observation law implies about the measurement process, most often UMI counts from single cells. Sec. 1 states the measurement and expression models that lens relies on. Sec. 2.2 states the errors-in-variables problem that every method solves, Sec. 2.3 orders the methods on a ladder of noise models, and Sec. 2.4 separates marginal from conditional multivariate models. The methods follow, grouped by what they estimate and what they assume known:

  1. reference-based estimation of the composition, split by whether genes are treated as independent (Sec. 2);
  2. cell-type-specific moments when the composition is known (Sec. 3);
  3. Bayesian reference-based methods, for profiles or for proportions (Sec. 4);
  4. semi-reference methods that infer one unknown component (Sec. 5);
  5. reference-free methods that use co-expression structure (Sec. 6).

Sec. 7 compares them and lists their caveats. The DeCovarT model rebuilt for single-cell references is in the single-cell generative vignette.

Measurement and expression models for single-cell counts

A reference profile is a moment of a latent biological quantity, but it is estimated from counts produced by a sampling protocol. Sarkar and Stephens separate the two: a measurement model p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}) describes the protocol given the true expression, an expression model p(\boldsymbol{\lambda}) describes the biology, and the observation model p(\boldsymbol{x}) is their composition (Sarkar and Stephens 2021). Fang and Pachter add that the cell-level scale factor is itself a product of a biological and a technical term (Fang and Pachter 2025). Both papers index genes by j and cells by i; below, gene is g and cell is c, so that j remains the cell type.

Poisson measurement of UMI counts

If each molecule of cell c is captured independently with a small probability, the multivariate hypergeometric sampling of molecules is close to a multinomial and each gene count is Poisson given the true content (Supplementary Note 1 of (Sarkar and Stephens 2021)):

x_{gc}\mid s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c,m_{gc} \sim\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c\,b_g\,m_{gc}\bigr), \qquad \boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}. \tag{1}

Fang and Pachter write the same law as binomial thinning with capture rate b_gs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c, of which the Poisson is the low-capture limit, and normalise \mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{bio}}]=\mathbb{E}[s^{\mathrm{tech}}]=1 (their equations 1–2). Sarkar and Stephens instead take the observed library size x_{+c} as the size factor and a relative expression \lambda_{gc}=m_{gc}/m_{+c}; in that convention s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c cancels by construction, which is the removal of biological extrinsic noise that Fang and Pachter warn about. The two conventions are the two directions of the same rank-one Poisson fit: the point-mass MLE \hat\mu_g=\sum_cx_{gc}/\sum_cx_{+c} and the size-factor MLE of Eq. 3 below.

Three remarks connect the protocol to deconvolution.

  • UMIs remove most gene-specific distortion. Unique molecular identifiers collapse PCR duplicates, which “substantially reduce unwanted variation, including differences in gene lengths and PCR amplification efficiencies” (Sarkar and Stephens 2021). What remains is a capture efficiency b_g that is constant across cells of one protocol. It is not identified separately from \boldsymbol{\lambda}, and it cancels from every within-protocol contrast, so it is absorbed into \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}. It does not cancel between a single-cell reference and a bulk library: the ratio \tilde b_g=b_g^{\mathrm{bulk}}/b_g^{\mathrm{ref}} is the gene-wise platform factor of plug-in scales (Strategy 4). Read-count protocols without UMIs and hybridisation microarrays carry larger gene- and probe-specific factors (amplification, length, affinity), which is why earlier deconvolution methods had to model gene-wise scales explicitly; with UMI references, the gene-wise factor reduces to one cross-platform ratio per gene.
  • Random capture biases make the measurement overdispersed; constant ones do not. If b_{gc} varied from cell to cell, the measurement model would be negative binomial rather than Poisson (Box 1 and Supplementary Note 1.2 of Sarkar and Stephens). On spike-in controls the measurement dispersion was below 5\times10^{-3}, which adds about 5% to the variance of a gene with ten observed molecules. Overdispersion seen in single-cell data is therefore an expression property, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j, plus extrinsic noise, not a protocol property.
  • Zero inflation belongs to the expression model, if anywhere. Spike-in controls show no zero-generating measurement component, and a point-Gamma expression model beats a Gamma model for only 0.6–8.6% of genes across the datasets tested (Sarkar and Stephens 2021). Zeros are imperfect measurements of small \lambda_{gc} at low depth, “with no need for special terminology or special treatment”. For DeCovarT, which uses only the first two moments of the reference, a zero-inflated observation model is unnecessary: the moments of the counts already contain the zeros. The argument is made for UMI data; the authors note that it may not hold for read counts amplified by PCR without UMIs.

Expression models and the observation models they induce

Integrating the expression model against Eq. 1 gives the observation model gene by gene (Table 1 of (Sarkar and Stephens 2021)).

A gene whose expression model is a point mass inside a homogeneous population is a Poisson gene: its count has no variability beyond sampling and the extrinsic size factor. Overdispersion relative to a Poisson, the hallmark of the negative binomial, then measures either biological variability of \lambda_{gc} or variability of s_c.

Extrinsic noise, size factors and Poisson genes

Fang and Pachter show that a cell-wide factor explains the baseline overdispersion of single-cell counts. Under Eq. 1 with s_c=s^{\mathrm{bio}}_cs^{\mathrm{tech}}_c independent of \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\cdot c}, \mathbb{E}[s_c]=1 and \nu=\operatorname{CV}^{2}(s_c), their equation (3) reads, in our notation and inside one cell type,

\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x_{gc},x_{hc})}{\mathbb{E}[x_{gc}]\mathbb{E}[x_{hc}]} =\nu+(1+\nu)\frac{\Sigma^{\lambda}_{j,gh}}{\tilde\mu_{gj}\tilde\mu_{hj}} +\frac{\delta_{gh}}{\mathbb{E}[x_{gc}]}, \qquad 1+\nu=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}). \tag{2}

For two genes that are intrinsically uncorrelated, or for one gene that is intrinsically Poisson, the normalised covariance equals \nu (their equation 5). That identity gives an estimator of \nu (the mode of the normalised covariances over gene pairs) and a selection rule for Poisson genes (those whose normalised variance minus the Poisson term has a bootstrap interval containing \hat\nu). On those genes \mathcal{P}, the size factor has the closed-form MLE

\hat s_c=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{P}}x_{gc}}{\sum_{g\in\mathcal{P}}\tilde\mu_{gj}}. \tag{3}

Two findings matter here. Normalising each cell by its total removes s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c together with s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c, and with it the biological extrinsic variability, including cell size (Fang and Pachter 2025). In peripheral blood, sums over Poisson genes no longer track total UMI counts and differ between cell types, so the choice of size factor changes downstream comparisons. Separating s^{\mathrm{tech}}_c from s^{\mathrm{bio}}_c needs external controls (spike-ins, ambient RNA, pooled RNA); the nascent-mRNA counts did not fit the binomial sampling model in their pooled-RNA experiment.

What the measurement model implies for the reference covariance

Write the same identity in matrix form (a direct consequence of Eq. 1 and the law of total covariance; the derivation is ours). With \boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}),

\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\mid c\in j) =\underbrace{\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\bigr)}_{\text{Poisson measurement}} +\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\Bigl[ \underbrace{(1+\nu)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j}_{\text{biology}} +\underbrace{\nu\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}}_{\text{size factor}} \Bigr]\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}. \tag{4}

The sample covariance of raw UMI counts, which is what a single-cell reference returns as \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}, mixes three objects. Only part of it belongs in the bulk law.

  1. The Poisson diagonal is single-cell measurement noise. It is produced at single-cell depth and is not part of the tissue. A bulk library has its own sampling noise, on its own depth, which a diagonal bulk term would carry. Plugging raw-count covariances into \boldsymbol{S}_W imports the reference sampling noise into the bulk covariance; subtracting \operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j) first removes it.
  2. The technical size-factor term is not biology either. The rank-one term \nu^{\mathrm{tech}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top} induces a positive correlation between all genes. It inflates the apparent network and is a protocol artefact.
  3. The biological size factor is part of the bulk. Cells of one type differ in volume and cycle phase; a tissue sums those cells as they are. The term \nu^{\mathrm{bio}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top} belongs in \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}, and library-size normalisation that removes it understates the within-type variance that the bulk accumulates.

The corresponding moment estimator, with \hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}} from spike-ins and \hat\kappa=\hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}/(1+\hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}), is

\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} =\boldsymbol{V}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j) -\hat\kappa\, \Bigl[\boldsymbol{V}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)+\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j^{\top}-\frac{\boldsymbol{V}_j}{C_j}\Bigr], \tag{5}

where \boldsymbol{V}_j is the unbiased sample covariance of the C_j type-j cells and \bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j their mean. It estimates the s^{\mathrm{tech}}-free covariance of \boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot c}, \boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}[(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}]\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}, obtained by solving Eq. 4 with 1+\nu=(1+\nu^{\mathrm{bio}})(1+\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}) (our derivation). Given \nu^{\mathrm{tech}} it is unbiased. The term -\boldsymbol{V}_j/C_j is needed because \bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j^{\top} overestimates the outer product of the means by \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x})/C_j; without it the estimator is biased by -\kappa\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x})/C_j, which a simulation with C_j=10 cells detects. The error of an estimated \hat\nu^{\mathrm{tech}} is not covered by this statement. Plugging in the total extrinsic noise \nu, which a size factor fitted on Poisson genes estimates (Sec. 1.3), returns \boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}: it removes the biological share \nu^{\mathrm{bio}}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\lambda}_j+\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}} with the technical one. Whether this denoised covariance enters the bulk alone or with the bulk’s own sampling term depends on the bulk depth per cell (raw or denoised). Estimating \nu^{\mathrm{tech}} before the deconvolution is the first plug-in of Strategy 4 (plug-in scales (Strategy 4)).

ComBat, scVI and scANVI: what they remove

Three families of correction are often proposed for the same job. Each removes a different quantity, on a different unit.

  • ComBat corrects “both additive and multiplicative batch effects” in an empirical-Bayes framework (Johnson, Li and Rabinovic 2007, as summarised by Zhang 2025, p. 1): a location and a scale per gene and batch, shrunk across genes. TODO-cite: Johnson, Li & Rabinovic 2007, Biostatistics 8(1):118-127, doi:10.1093/biostatistics/kxj037; Zhang, Parmigiani & Johnson 2020, ComBat-seq, NAR Genom Bioinform 2(3), doi:10.1093/nargab/lqaa078; Zhang 2025, ComBat-ref, Comput Struct Biotechnol J 27:58-64, doi:10.1016/j.csbj.2024.12.010. None is in inst/REFERENCES.bib. Its count version, ComBat-ref, fits \log\mu_{gij}=\alpha_g+\gamma_{gi}+\beta_{g,\mathrm{cond}(j)}+\log N_j for gene g, batch i and sample j with a pooled negative binomial dispersion per batch, keeps the batch of smallest dispersion as reference, sets \log\tilde\mu_{gij}=\log\mu_{gij}+\gamma_{g1}-\gamma_{gi}, and maps each count by matching negative binomial distribution functions, zeros to zeros (Zhang 2025, p. 2). The unit is a bulk sample inside a batch; the biological condition is a term of the model, and single-cell data are left to future work (p. 6).
  • scVI draws, for cell n, a latent \boldsymbol{z}_n\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\mathbf{I}), a library factor \ell_n\sim\mathrm{LogNormal} whose prior is the empirical mean and variance of the log library size of its batch, frequencies \boldsymbol{\rho}_n=f_w(\boldsymbol{z}_n,s_n) that sum to one over genes, and counts \mathrm{Poisson}(\ell_nw_{ng}) with w_{ng}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\rho_{gn},\theta_g), plus zero inflation (Lopez et al. 2018, author manuscript pp. 8–9). \ell_n “represents nuisance variation due to differences in capture efficiency and sequencing depth”, and the batch s_n enters the decoder, so \rho_{ng} is “a batch-corrected, normalized estimate of the percentage of transcripts” (p. 3). Genes are independent given (\boldsymbol{z}_n,\ell_n) (p. 8), so gene–gene covariance passes through the 10-dimensional \boldsymbol{z}_n only (p. 3). No reference is used. TODO-cite: Lopez, Regier, Cole, Jordan & Yosef 2018, Nat Methods 15(12):1053-1058, doi:10.1038/s41592-018-0229-2; not in inst/REFERENCES.bib.
  • scANVI adds a cell-type label c_n with a uniform prior, a within-type latent \boldsymbol{u}_n and \boldsymbol{z}_n\sim\mathcal{N}(f_\mu(\boldsymbol{u}_n,c_n),f_\sigma(\boldsymbol{u}_n,c_n)), with the scVI library factor and count model unchanged (Xu et al. 2021, equations 1–8, p. 15). Labels of an annotated reference are transferred to the cells of other datasets (pp. 2–3). TODO-cite: Xu, Lopez, Mehlman, Regier, Jordan & Yosef 2021, Mol Syst Biol 17:e9620, doi:10.15252/msb.20209620; not in inst/REFERENCES.bib.

Our setting differs on three points (our reading).

  1. One reference specimen. There is no second batch for \gamma_{gi} or for the batch covariate s_n. With one specimen only the cell-wide factor (s_c, or scVI’s \ell_n) can be estimated.
  2. The target is the bulk, at its own depth. The question is which part of the reference second moments a deeper bulk inherits, not how to map one dataset onto another. Eq. 5 removes the Poisson and technical size-factor shares from the covariance; it changes no count and aligns no batch.
  3. The biological size factor must stay. scVI’s frequencies sum to one, so \ell_n absorbs the whole cell-wide factor, cell size included: the moment analogue is the total-\nu plug-in above, which drops \nu^{\mathrm{bio}}. Its gene–gene covariance is also of rank at most the latent dimension, whereas \boldsymbol{S}_W needs a full-rank \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}.

What carries over is the empirical-Bayes pooling. \nu^{\mathrm{tech}} is a property of the protocol, shared by genes and cell types, so per-pair estimates from normalised covariances can be shrunk towards one common value instead of taking their mode; with several specimens, ComBat’s gene-wise location shrinkage is the model for a pooled platform ratio \tilde b_g. What does not carry over is the mapping of counts: a quantile map of each count, like a logarithm, is non-linear and breaks the additive mixture of the bulk (normalisation that preserves the linear mixture).

Before single cells: measurement models for sorted population profiles

Before droplet single-cell sequencing, a reference column was a bulk measurement of a physically sorted population: FACS or magnetic sorting, then a microarray or a bulk RNA-seq library. The measurement model was the one of the platform, applied to a pool of many cells.

  • Microarrays. A probe intensity is a background plus a probe-specific affinity times the abundance, with errors that are roughly additive at low intensity and multiplicative at high intensity. Analyses of differential expression worked on \log_2 intensities, where the multiplicative error becomes additive. Deconvolution could not: mixing is additive in the abundance, so the first reference-based methods fitted linear models on unlogged intensities (Abbas et al. 2009; Shen-Orr et al. 2010; Lähdesmäki et al. 2005). The probe affinity is a gene-wise factor of the platform. It cancels within one platform and does not cancel between platforms, which is the origin of the gene-wise platform ratio \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} of later methods.
  • Bulk RNA-seq of sorted populations. Reads are counts with a library size and a gene-length factor (for full-length protocols). Replicate libraries of one sorted population vary by a negative binomial dispersion that mixes biological and technical variation. Normalised counts on a linear scale (CPM, TPM) became the default input, with the same warning against logarithms.
  • What the reference variance meant. With a handful of sorted replicates per population, the only second-order quantity available was a between-replicate variance of the population mean. That is the quadratic layer \sum_jp_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j} of the single-cell generative vignette, and the covariance of the purified-profile paradigm. A within-type, cell-to-cell covariance did not exist in that design.

Two biases of sorted references have no single-cell analogue: sorting selects cells on a few surface markers, so a “pure” population can contain contaminating types; and the sorting itself can change expression before lysis. Single-cell references remove the first by labelling cells after the fact, and replace the platform model by the Poisson measurement of Sec. 1.1.

From measurement models to bulk observation laws

A deconvolution method chooses a law for the bulk. Read with the split of Sec. 1, that law is a measurement model (multinomial, Poisson) composed with an expression model for the purified profiles (Gaussian, log-normal, Gamma). The support of \boldsymbol{y} is the first split: count laws for integer reads, continuous laws for normalised intensities. Table 3 places every reviewed method on a ladder of noise models that crosses that split; the count laws are detailed here because they sit closest to the measurement model.

Discrete counts

A multinomial (or Dirichlet–multinomial) model treats \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i} as integer reads that sum to a library size. ISOpureR implements a hierarchical multinomial–Dirichlet purification of mixed tumour profiles (Anghel et al. 2015). BayesPrism is the multinomial model with a single-cell prior (Sec. 4.1). DeconV instead uses Poisson aggregation from single-cell to bulk (sums of independent Poissons remain Poisson) and returns interval estimates of \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} (Gynter et al. 2023) (Sec. 2.5.8). RCTD is a Poisson–log-normal mixture of reads (Sec. 2.5.7).

Over-dispersed, correlated counts are the domain of the multivariate Poisson–log-normal (PLN) family: a latent Gaussian vector induces dependence, and a Poisson observation layer yields integer reads (Chiquet et al. 2021, 2018). ZIPLN adds a Bernoulli zero-inflation layer for dropout (Batardière et al. 2025). A DeCovarT-style extension would replace Eq. 20 by a PLN (or ZIPLN) convolution on the latent log-abundance scale, keeping the ILR chart on \boldsymbol{p}. A multinomial logit-normal on the gene simplex is a different discrete model: it is compositional association, not a cell-type convolution (two simplices without convolution).

Second-generation deconvolution: univariate versus multivariate

Second-generation methods use a single-cell reference and model, in some form, the variability of the cell-type profiles. The usual split into regression and probabilistic engines hides the property that matters for DeCovarT: whether the bulk model treats genes as independent (a diagonal variance per gene) or keeps a gene–gene covariance. Figure 2 uses that split.

A common notation

Each paper uses its own indices; several use j for the gene or the subject. Table 2 maps them to this vignette. The scale columns show how one model is reparametrised into another by arithmetic alone.

Three reparametrisations recur.

  • Counts to fractions. A model in cell counts, \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}, becomes a model in fractions after division by the number of cells, \tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. RNA-Sieve keeps n_i as a parameter; DWLS estimates \boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i} (its “cell-type numbers”) and normalises at the end.
  • Total molecules to average cell size. MuSiC equation (2) gives \sum_gX_{gi}=n_i\sum_jp_{ji}S_j. Dividing by n_i gives the average cell size of the sample, \bar S_i=\sum_jp_{ji}S_j, and MuSiC’s normalising constant is its inverse, \kappa_i=\bar S_i^{-1}. Library-size normalisation therefore returns transcript fractions q_{ji}=p_{ji}S_j/\bar S_i, not cell fractions.
  • Scale times composition. MEAD estimates \boldsymbol{\beta}_i=a_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and RCTD p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}; both normalise at the end. The total of the unnormalised weights identifies the sample scale (the sample-wide capture scale).

The common problem: errors in variables

Every method of this review estimates a composition from two noisy views of one latent truth: the purified profile \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i} of each type in each sample. The bulk mixes these profiles; the reference supplies only an estimate of their mean:

\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i, \qquad \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}+\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}, \qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}+\boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j}, \tag{6}

with three mean-zero errors: the biological deviation \boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i} of sample i from the type mean, the measurement noise \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i of the bulk library, and the estimation error \boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j} of a reference built from finitely many cells or donors. Substituting the reference gives the regression that every method fits, \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{e}_i with \boldsymbol{e}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}(\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}-\boldsymbol{v}_{\cdot j})+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i: an errors-in-variables model whose regressor is the reference. The methods differ by two choices.

  • Where the error is modelled. \boldsymbol{v} is an error in the regressor, the classical errors-in-variables layer; ignoring it biases \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} (attenuation, in the linear case) and understates its variance. RNA-Sieve models it in a joint likelihood and MEAD removes it with a bias-corrected estimating equation; every other method plugs \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} in as exact and models the response error \sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{u}_{\cdot j,i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i only.
  • How the error is specified. By a parametric law (Gaussian in DeCovarT, Poisson–log-normal in RCTD, Poisson in DeconV), by an asymptotic law (the central limit over the n_i cells of a sample in RNA-Sieve and ReDeconv; over genes, G\to\infty, in MEAD and DECALS), or by its first two conditional moments only, \mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{e}_i\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})=\boldsymbol{0} and a working \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{e}_i\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}), the route by which least squares is justified without a Gaussian assumption (Agresti 2015, ch. 2). Sec. 2.3 orders these choices.

The textbook assumptions do not hold here. The classical model takes the errors independent of the true regressor and of each other, with a constant variance (terminology and assumptions). In DeCovarT the response error has covariance \sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, a function of the parameter; in Poisson models (RCTD, DeconV) the variance equals the mean, again a function of \boldsymbol{p}. Our reading: once the type mean is assigned and the sample profile scatters around it independently of that mean, the \boldsymbol{u} layer is a Berkson error, which does not bias a linear estimator but enters weighted by the coefficients p_{ji}, hence heteroscedastically. The \boldsymbol{v} layer is classical, and DeCovarT ignores it by plugging in \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}, which is defensible only when every type has many reference cells.

A ladder of noise models

All the methods share a mean linear in \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. They differ in what they assume about the response error \boldsymbol{e}_i of Eq. 6. Ordered by how much of \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{e}_i\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}) they model, the assumptions form a ladder. Each rung keeps the mean and changes the variance model, the estimator, or the source of the interval (Agresti 2015, chs 2, 4, 8 and 9).

  1. Ordinary or non-negative least squares. \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{e}_i)=\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}_G: one variance for all genes, no correlation.
  2. Weighted least squares. \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{e}_i)=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma^{2}_{gi}), with the marginal variances taken from the reference, from the fitted mean or from residuals. Genes stay uncorrelated.
  3. Mean–variance generalised linear model. The law is an exponential family (Poisson, negative binomial, multinomial) whose variance is a known function of the mean, \operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})=\varphi\,V\bigl((\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g\bigr) (Nelder and Wedderburn 1972); DeCovarT read as a GLM is in the population inference vignette.
  4. Quasi-likelihood or asymptotic Gaussian. Only the first two moments are specified, and the variance may depend on \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} through more than the mean, linearly, as in \sum_jp_{ji}\operatorname{Var}(x_{gc}\mid c\in j), or quadratically, as in Unico’s \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2} (Sec. 3.2). Over the n_i cells of a bulk sample the central limit theorem turns these moments into a Gaussian working likelihood. When genes are still treated as independent, the product over genes is a composite likelihood, and its intervals need the Godambe sandwich (Godambe 1960).
  5. Generalised least squares with a dense covariance. \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{e}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i is a full G\times G matrix, known or plugged in. When \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i does not depend on \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}, GLS is the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate of \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. When it does, as in \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, the Gaussian likelihood adds a log-determinant term and is no longer a weighted least-squares criterion (GLS competitor).
  6. Sandwich and generalised estimating equations (GEE). The mean is fitted under a working covariance (identity or diagonal), and the dependence the working model omits enters only the sandwich variance (Liang and Zeger 1986 TODO-cite: Liang and Zeger 1986, doi:10.1093/biomet/73.1.13). The point estimate stays consistent when the mean is right; the interval is valid only when the units summed in the “meat” of the sandwich are numerous and nearly independent. Classical GEE takes those units to be independent clusters; DECALS and MEAD take them to be the genes of one sample, with G\to\infty and a sparse dependency graph, which is why dense gene correlation breaks their coverage (Sec. 2.6.1).
  7. Generalised linear mixed model (GLMM). Latent random effects, gene-wise or sample-wise, generate the overdispersion and the correlation, and the law of \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i} is obtained by integrating them out (Agresti 2015, ch. 9).

?@fig-ladder draws the seven rungs, with the methods of this review placed on each, including Unico (Sec. 3.2), DeconV (Sec. 2.5.8), imply (Sec. 3.3) and BLEND (Sec. 4.1.1).

Errors in variables cuts across the ladder: the regressor error \boldsymbol{v} of Eq. 6 can be added on any rung, as a joint likelihood (RNA-Sieve, rung 4), a bias-corrected estimating equation (MEAD, rung 6) or a prior on the signature (BEDwARS, rung 1).

Moment estimators give point estimates. Weighted non-negative least squares (MuSiC, SCDC, DWLS, deMixSC) solves the normal equations \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})=\boldsymbol{0}, and Unico matches first and second sample moments explicitly. All are generalised method of moments estimators: consistent under correct moment conditions, but they return a point estimate only. An interval needs a higher rung: a sandwich (DECALS, MEAD), a likelihood (RNA-Sieve, DeCovarT) or a resampling unit (genes, cells or donors). When the weights are re-estimated from the residuals of the same fit (MuSiC, deMixSC), the nominal weighted-least-squares covariance is not valid either (our remark).

Families of multivariate models

Here multivariate means several correlated responses per unit, the G genes of one bulk sample; it is not multivariable, which refers to several explanatory variables. Rungs 5 to 7 need a joint law, or at least a joint covariance, for those G responses. Two families supply one (Agresti 2015, sec. 9.1).

  • Marginal models specify \mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}) and the dependence between genes directly. An explicit joint law that accepts any positive-definite covariance and stays in its family under marginalisation and conditioning is essentially the Gaussian, with its scale mixtures such as the multivariate t, where a zero in the precision no longer means conditional independence (our summary). For counts, many joint laws share the same margins, none is canonical, and the number of parameters grows quickly: a trivariate Poisson built from sums of independent Poisson variables already needs seven of them (Olkin 1994, pp. 37 and 42–43 TODO-cite: Olkin 1994, IMS Lecture Notes-Monograph Series 24, pp. 37-53, no DOI (JSTOR 4355792)). A marginal model of bulk expression therefore takes one of three routes: an asymptotic Gaussian (RNA-Sieve, ReDeconv, DeCovarT single-cell); moments only, through quasi-likelihood or GEE (DECALS, MEAD); or a copula, which couples chosen univariate margins into a full likelihood (none of the reviewed deconvolution methods).
  • Conditional models specify the law given latent effects and let shared effects induce the correlation: the GLMMs of rung 7 (RCTD, BayesPrism) and the Poisson–log-normal family of
    1. The integrated margins leave the conditional family (a Poisson–log-normal count is not Poisson), and a zero in the latent precision is a conditional independence between latent log-expressions, not between counts.

For Gaussian responses with an identity link the two families meet. A linear mixed model \boldsymbol{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{Z}\boldsymbol{u}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, with \boldsymbol{u}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\mathbf{G}_u) and \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\mathbf{R}), implies the marginal model \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{G}_u\mathbf{Z}^{\top}+\mathbf{R}), whose fixed effects GLS estimates (Agresti 2015, sec. 9.2–9.3). DeCovarT sits at that point: its Gaussian convolution is a marginal model and, read conditionally, a linear mixed model whose random-effect design depends on \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} (LMM reading). With a non-identity link the conditional and the population-averaged coefficients differ, so a count-scale DeCovarT would have to choose between the two families.

Univariate methods: genes independent

MuSiC starts from molecules: the bulk of subject i holds X_{gi}=\sum_jm_{ji}S_j\theta_{gj}=\sum_jm_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}, with S_j the mean total molecules per cell of type j (equation 2). It works on relative abundance Y_{gi}=X_{gi}/\sum_{g'}X_{g'i}, so that, with the reparametrisation above,

Y_{gi}=\kappa_i\Bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}S_j\theta_{gj}+\varepsilon_{gi}\Bigr), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_{gi}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}) =\kappa_i^{2}\delta_{gi}^{2}+\kappa_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}S_j^{2}\sigma^{2}_{gj} =w_{gi}^{-1} \tag{7}

(equations 8–10). The second term comes from subject-level relative profiles \theta_{gj,i}\sim F(\theta_{gj},\sigma^{2}_{gj}) (assumption A1): it is the diagonal of the between-replicate layer \boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p}), quadratic in p_{ji}, and it requires a multi-subject reference. Cross terms between types are dropped, which implicitly assumes independence across types. \delta^{2}_{gi} is the residual variance of the bulk. The within-type cell scatter \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} has no term in Eq. 7; it is used only to select genes with small within-cluster variance in the tree-guided recursion; the cross-subject weights and the cross-cell selection are the two halves of what the paper calls marker-gene consistency (p. 2). Estimation is weighted non-negative least squares, with the weights updated from an initial fit because \delta^{2}_{gi} is unknown, followed by rescaling to the simplex.

Scales and identifiability. S_j is plugged in as the mean library size of type j in the reference. That substitution returns cell fractions only under assumption A3', a capture efficiency (observed library size over molecule content) common to all types (the MuSiC assumptions); otherwise MuSiC estimates the RNA-weighted product p_{ji}S_j. Under A1–A3 alone the paper claims only the trend of proportions across subjects. Absolute S_j is not needed: it cancels into \kappa_i. A gene- and subject-specific intercept \alpha_{gi} absorbs protocol bias. MuSiC2 keeps the weights and removes genes that are differentially expressed between the reference and bulk conditions (Fan et al. 2022).

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 2; response error only, with a diagonal variance quadratic in \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}; \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} is plugged in, and the estimator is a weighted moment estimator.

SCDC

SCDC keeps the weighted non-negative least squares of MuSiC and changes the weights and the reference (Dong et al. 2021). Each gene receives a maximal variance weight, “so that residuals from genes with larger weights have smaller impact” (p. 5): as we read the formula (garbled in our copy, p. 9), the largest cross-cell variance of the gene over the cell types of one reference subject, divided by its median over genes. Weights below the 15th percentile are raised to it and weights above the 85th percentile are lowered to it (p. 10), so the clipping is a percentile rule, not an influence diagnostic. With several single-cell references, SCDC fits each one separately and combines the estimates with data-set weights chosen to fit the bulk (its ENSEMBLE step). No interval for \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} is reported.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 2; response error only; a weighted moment estimator with no interval.

RNA-Sieve

(a) With known per-cell moments $(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{\varsigma}^{2})$, the bulk is the sum of $n_i$ cells drawn from the cell mixture, with a central-limit Gaussian per gene whose variance is the mixture variance. (b) The reference means are themselves noisy averages of $C_j$ cells; the joint likelihood over bulks and reference means is maximised, with Godambe sandwich intervals.

Panel b: the same, plus an observed noisy reference mean generated by mu tilde, varsigma squared and the fixed number of reference cells C_j.

RNA-Sieve writes the bulk as a sum of n cells, each a draw from the cell mixture the mixture-of-cells covariance restricted to one gene. By the central limit theorem,

y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(n_i(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g,\ n_i\sigma^{2}_{gi}\bigr), \qquad \sigma^{2}_{gi}=\sum_jp_{ji}\bigl(\varsigma^{2}_{gj}+\tilde\mu_{gj}^{2}\bigr)-(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})_g^{2}, \tag{8}

with genes independent (equations 5–8). The variance is linear in n_i and in \boldsymbol{p}, minus the square of the mixture mean: the within-type variance \sum_jp_{ji}\varsigma^{2}_{gj} plus the spread of the type means, the diagonal of the mixture-of-cells covariance. The reference means are noisy, \hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\sim\mathcal{N}(\tilde\mu_{gj},\varsigma^{2}_{gj}/C_j) (equation 9), and the true means are estimated jointly with (\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},n_i) from all bulks (equations 10–11). Marginalising them instead would add n_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\varsigma^{2}_{gj}/C_j to the variance, a quadratic term that vanishes as the reference grows (our remark).

Here \varsigma^{2}_{gj} is the per-cell variance of gene g in type j, the diagonal of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}.

Scales. Raw counts keep S_j inside \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}, so the weights are cell fractions; the optional rescaling of every cell to the median library size removes S_j and turns them into RNA fractions. Any global protocol difference is absorbed into n_i, which then “loses interpretability” as a cell number across protocols (Supplementary S1.4). The optional cell QC drops cells whose library size lies 3 median absolute deviations or more from the median of their type; the gene filters are compared in the feature-selection review.

Intervals. When the model holds, the inverse Fisher information of (\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i},\hat n_i), after a reparametrisation of the simplex, gives \chi^{2}_{J-1} ellipsoids. Under protocol shift the data law leaves the model family, and the default Godambe sandwich describes the fluctuations around the Kullback–Leibler projection onto that family; without misspecification the two matrices coincide (Godambe 1960). Near-collinear cell types make the information nearly singular. The paper notes that gene correlation “may be incorporated” once it is known, but does not implement it: the product over genes is a composite likelihood.

Against DeCovarT. DeCovarT draws one latent profile per type and keeps a full gene–gene covariance, \sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, where RNA-Sieve sums n_i cells gene by gene. DeCovarT already has the Fisher analogue, the expected information mapped through the ILR chart (interior intervals), undefined on a face of the simplex. A Godambe correction matters only if the Gaussian convolution is misspecified (counts, protocol shift, omitted types); its one-column construction is a proposal, not implemented (sandwich for a misspecified convolution). It replaces neither the boundary tests nor reference_bootstrap_decovart(), the resampling counterpart of the noisy-reference term.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 4, a composite asymptotic Gaussian; both layers, the response error with a central-limit law over cells and the regressor error in a joint likelihood.

DWLS 

%%| label: fig-dag-dwls
%%| fig-cap: `DWLS` [@tsoucasAccurateEstimationCelltype2019]. The signature is the average of reference cells; the bulk is fitted in cell-type numbers $\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i}$ by iterated weighted least squares, with weights equal to the inverse squared fitted mean, capped by a dampening constant $w_{\max}$.

\plate{i}{(m)(w)(y)(ny)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}

DWLS fits the cell-type numbers \mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i} by

\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i} =\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{m}\ge\boldsymbol{0}}\sum_g\bar w_{gi}\bigl(y_{gi}-\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}\bigr)^{2}, \qquad \bar w_{gi}=\min\Bigl\{w_{\max},\ \frac{(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i})^{-2}}{\min_{g'}(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g'\cdot}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}_{\cdot i})^{-2}}\Bigr\}, \tag{9}

iterated from an ordinary least squares start, with w_{\max}=2^{q} chosen to minimise the variance of estimates over random half-gene subsets (equations 6–15). The purpose is stated on p. 7: with weights 1/(\text{fitted expression})^{2} the loss becomes a function of the relative error of each cell type, “because we would like all cell types to be estimated with equal accuracy”; highly expressed genes, which dominate an unweighted fit and favour abundant types, are down-weighted. Read as a variance model, the weights imply \operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})\propto(\hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}_{g\cdot}\boldsymbol{m}_{\cdot i})^{2}, a constant coefficient of variation, which the paper does not state. There is no \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} term and genes are independent. \mathbf{x} are cell numbers only under equal RNA per cell; otherwise they are RNA-weighted.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 2, with a variance proportional to the squared mean (the variance function of a gamma GLM, our reading); response error only; a weighted moment estimator with no interval.

deMixSC

deMixSC keeps the weighted non-negative least squares of MuSiC and DWLS and adds a small benchmark data set: bulk and single-nucleus libraries prepared from the same nucleus aliquot, so that the real bulk and the pseudo-bulk share the composition (Guo et al. 2025, p. 149 TODO-cite: Guo et al. 2025, Genome Research, doi:10.1101/gr.278822.123; page numbers below refer to it; preprint Guo et al. (2023)). In the 24 benchmark retinas, more than 5000 genes differ between the two platforms in each batch, and TPM normalisation does not remove the difference. In our notation the working model is (supplementary note, equations S.1–S.5, pp. 1–2)

y_{gi}=n_i\sum_jp_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj}+\epsilon_{gi}, \qquad \tilde\mu_{gj}=S_j\theta_{gj}, \qquad \hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}=\tilde\mu_{gj}+\bar\xi_{gj}, \tag{10}

with mean-zero bulk noise \epsilon_{gi} and an averaged single-cell measurement error \bar\xi_{gj}. The residual of a fit with \hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}} is the estimation error plus a “technological discrepancy” between platforms (note, p. 3). Two changes to weighted NNLS follow.

  • Partitioned loss (equation S.7, note p. 3). Genes differentially expressed between real bulk and pseudo-bulk in the benchmark (paired t-test, Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted P<0.05, the 5000 most expressed of them by default) form a set G_2. They are kept, not removed: their bulk value and reference are divided by a constant a (1000 by default), which scales their squared residuals by a^{-2}:

    \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{p}\ge\boldsymbol{0}} \sum_{g\in G_1}w_{gi}\,r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})^{2} +\frac{1}{a^{2}}\sum_{g\in G_2}w_{gi}\,r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})^{2}, \qquad r_{gi}(\boldsymbol{p})=y_{gi}-n_i\sum_jp_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}. \tag{11}

  • Weights (equation S.9, note p. 3; main text p. 150): w_{gi}^{-1}=\hat y_{gi}^{2}+(y_{gi}-\hat y_{gi})^{2}+c, with \hat y_{gi}=n_i\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} and c=2. Earlier methods, the authors note, use “either the squared fitted value” (DWLS, Eq. 9) “or the variance” (MuSiC’s iteratively estimated \delta^{2}_{gi}, Eq. 7), “but never both” (p. 157). The fit is iterated from an NNLS start (note, p. 4).

The target cohort is first aligned to the benchmark bulk by quantile normalisation and ComBat (p. 150). The platform effect is treated as noise to down-weight, not as a gene-wise ratio \tilde b_g to estimate: with a=1000 the genes of G_2 receive a weight 10^{-6} times smaller, which nearly discards them. The squared residual in the weight uses one residual per gene as its own variance, an outlier-damping device in the spirit of robust M-estimation rather than a variance model (our reading). Cell size enters through \tilde\mu_{gj}=S_j\theta_{gj}, as in MuSiC, so \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} are cell fractions under the same equal-efficiency assumption. No interval is reported.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 2; both layers are written down but enter only through the weights; a weighted moment estimator with no interval.

Bisque learns the platform shift instead of modelling it. In paired mode it fits y^{\mathrm{ps}}_{gi'}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_gy_{gi'}+\epsilon_{gi'} per gene, with \boldsymbol{y}^{\mathrm{ps}}_{\cdot i'}=\boldsymbol{\theta}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i'} the pseudo-bulk of individual i' (equation 1); in unpaired mode it matches the first two moments of each gene across samples (equations 2–3). The transformed bulk is then fitted by non-negative least squares with a sum-to-one constraint. The fitting step has homoscedastic residuals; the variability of the reference enters only through the between-sample moments used in the map. Because \boldsymbol{\theta} is built from CPM, cell size is removed from the signature; the gene-wise affine map absorbs the platform ratio \tilde b_g (as 1/\beta_g) and an intercept, not a type-specific S_j. In unpaired mode the cohort mean composition is assumed equal to the mean composition of the single-cell individuals.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 1; the platform error is removed by a learned map, then a homoscedastic moment estimator; no interval.

Perspective: two-scale transport beyond the gene-wise map

Perspective

Not implemented. DeCovarT learns its sample scales inside the likelihood (2.1, alignment; 2.1, profile Newton). This subsection says what a richer alignment would add.

Bisque states its goal per gene: “For each gene j, our goal is to transform the observed bulk expression across all n bulk samples X_j\in\mathbb{R}^n to match the mean and variance of Y_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n'}; hence, the transformation of X_j will be a linear transformation” (Jew et al. 2020, 10). Here Y_j is the pseudo-bulk of the n' single-cell individuals. Without pairs, the map is X_{j,\mathrm{transformed}}=(X_j-\bar X_j)\,\hat\sigma_j/\sigma_{X_j}+\bar Y_j, with \hat\sigma_j^{2} a shrunk variance of Y_j (equations 2–3, p. 10). The authors name the price: “a key assumption of our transformation framework is that single-cell-based estimates of cell proportions accurately reflect the true proportions we wish to estimate” (p. 9).

Our reading, not the authors’: equation 3 is, gene by gene, the optimal transport map between two univariate Gaussians. Between \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{m}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1) and \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{m}_2,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2) the quadratic-cost map is affine,

T(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{m}_2+\boldsymbol{A}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{m}_1), \qquad \boldsymbol{A}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1/2}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1/2}, \tag{12}

with cost W_2^2=\lVert\boldsymbol{m}_1-\boldsymbol{m}_2\rVert^2+\operatorname{tr}\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2-2(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{1/2})^{1/2}\} (Knott and Smith 1984; Dowson and Landau 1982). TODO-cite: Knott & Smith 1984, On the optimal mapping of distributions, J. Optim. Theory Appl. 43:39-49; Dowson & Landau 1982, The Frechet distance between multivariate normal distributions, J. Multivariate Anal. 12:450-455. Neither is in inst/REFERENCES.bib. For diagonal covariances \boldsymbol{A} is diagonal with entries \sigma_{2g}/\sigma_{1g}, which is Bisque’s map. Bisque is thus Gaussian transport with genes independent, applied to the law of the mixed bulk across samples. That law depends on the composition of each cohort, hence the assumption quoted above.

Transport of type-level laws avoids the composition. With the hierarchy of 2.1, three regimes there are two laws per type, and so two scales (?@fig-two-scale-ot):

  • cell scale: cells of type j in specimen r, \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{M}_{jr},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}). A map S_j aligns them across single-cell platforms, for example nuclei against whole cells;
  • type scale: type-level profiles across specimens, \mathcal{N}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}). A map T_j carries this law to the bulk platform, against an external population Gaussian such as sorted profiles or a many-donor pseudo-bulk atlas.

The mean of C cells has covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}/C, so S_j and T_j differ even when the two covariances share structure; one transport does not serve both. The three maps form a ladder:

Any map richer than a scalar absorbs \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} if it is fitted on the bulk sample being deconvolved (2.1, alignment). It needs paired samples, an external cohort or an external population law. With one reference specimen \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j} is not identified (2.1, one replicate), so T_j needs that external law. DecOT uses transport differently, as a loss between count histograms for the composition (Liu et al. 2022).

%%| label: fig-two-scale-ot
%%| fig-cap: Two-scale transport for one cell type $j$ (perspective). Each specimen $r$ draws a type-level profile $\boldsymbol{M}_{jr}$ from $\mathcal{N}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B,j})$ (type scale); its cells scatter around it with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}$ (cell scale). The map $S_j$ carries latent cells to the reference platform. The map $T_j$ pushes the type-level law to the bulk platform, where bulk sample $i$ mixes the transported profiles; $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i$ collects within-type cell noise and bulk measurement noise. `Bisque` instead applies a diagonal map to the mixed bulk.

RCTD

RCTD works one layer below DeCovarT. Each UMI first picks a type with probability p_{ji}, then a gene from that type’s relative profile: a read-level mixture, not a convolution of random population profiles (Cable et al. 2022). Given the rate, gene counts are Poisson; the rate is log-normal around a linear mixture of the fixed normalised means \theta_{gj} (supplementary equations 3, 22):

y_{gi}\mid\lambda_{gi}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(L_i\lambda_{gi}), \qquad \log\lambda_{gi}=\alpha_i+\log\Bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}\theta_{gj}\Bigr)+\gamma_g+\varepsilon_{gi}, \tag{13}

with L_i the observed depth, \alpha_i a leftover sample scale, \gamma_g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\gamma^{2}) a gene-specific platform random effect and \varepsilon_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^{2}) an observation-level random effect, with heavier tails in practice (p. 6). The model is a Poisson–log-normal GLMM. The Poisson mean is

\mathbb{E}[y_{gi}\mid\varepsilon_{gi}] =\underbrace{L_ie^{\alpha_i}}_{a_i}\,\tilde b_g\,e^{\varepsilon_{gi}}\sum_jp_{ji}\theta_{gj}, \qquad \tilde b_g=e^{\gamma_g}, \tag{14}

so the platform effect is exactly the gene-wise ratio \tilde b_g of Sec. 1.1, and \varepsilon_{gi} is the count-scale analogue of a diagonal bulk residual. Genes are independent given \varepsilon. In the language of the measurement model, the rate of gene g is a type-weighted sum of per-type rates scaled by one sample-wide factor; the same holds in DeCovarT’s single-cell mean a_in_i\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}, whose per-type contribution is n_ip_{ji}S_j molecules of profile \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j} (our reading). A mixture is the right story at the UMI; a convolution of random profiles (Eq. 20) is the right story for population profiles.

%%| label: fig-rctd-two-stage
%%| fig-cap: `RCTD` estimation. Stage 1 identifies the gene-wise platform ratio from a pseudobulk of all samples; stage 2 fits each sample by sequential quadratic programming on the unnormalised weights $w_{ji}=p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}$.
%%| filename: fig-rctd-two-stage
%%| alt: Flowchart. Library-normalised cells are averaged to theta hat; differentially expressed genes are kept; together with a pseudobulk of all samples they enter stage 1, a maximum-likelihood fit of the platform ratio b tilde and a bulk-wide mixture. The estimates are plugged into the Poisson-log-normal model; stage 2 runs a per-sample SQP on non-negative weights, which are normalised to give p hat.
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.append style={text width=3.4cm}]
\node[box] (avg) at (0,0) {average library-normalised cells to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\cdot j}$};
\node[box] (filt) at (0,-1.7) {keep differentially expressed genes};
\node[box] (pool) at (4.4,-1.7) {pool all samples into one pseudobulk};
\node[keybox] (s1) at (2.2,-3.6) {Stage 1: MLE of platform $\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ and a bulk-wide mixture};

The fit is two-stage because \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} cannot be free inside one sample (alignment scales): stage 1 estimates \sigma_\gamma and predicts \gamma_g from one pseudobulk of all spots (supplementary equations 14–19), stage 2 holds it fixed. That is Strategy 4 in its purest form (plug-in scales). Stage 2 maximises a non-convex Poisson–log-normal likelihood in w_{ji}=p_{ji}e^{\alpha_i}\ge0 by sequential quadratic programming: the Hessian is replaced by its positive-semidefinite part and each step is a constrained quadratic programme with step size 0.3. Zeros on the orthant boundary are native to that formulation, which suits spots with few types. DeCovarT instead maps \boldsymbol{p} to the ILR chart and takes Newton–Raphson steps with the analytic score and Hessian of a Gaussian law.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 7, a Poisson–log-normal GLMM; response error only; the reference means are plugged in and the platform effect is predicted in stage 1, then held fixed.

DeconV 

%%| label: fig-dag-deconv
%%| fig-cap: `DeconV` [@gynterDeconvProbabilisticCellType2023] in this vignette's notation, Poisson ("gamma") variant. Right, the bulk model: the fitted hyperparameters give a Gamma rate $\theta_{gj}$ per type, the proportions follow a Dirichlet whose concentration $\boldsymbol{N}$ is fitted, and the bulk count is Poisson with a mean linear in $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$. The negative-binomial variant replaces $\theta_{gj}$ by a log-normal $r_{gj}$ and adds a gene-wise $P_g$ shared by all types.

DeconV fits a count model to the single-cell reference, then aggregates it to the bulk (Gynter et al. 2023). The reference model (equations 1–2, p. 6) takes the counts of a cell c of type j as zero-inflated Poisson, x_{gc}\sim\mathrm{ZIPoisson}(\lambda_{gj},d_j), or zero-inflated negative binomial, \mathrm{ZINB}(r_{gj},P_g,d_j), with priors \lambda_{gj}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_{gj},\beta_{gj}), r_{gj}\sim\mathrm{LogNormal}(\mu_{gj},\sigma_{gj}) and P_g\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha_g,\beta_g). The hyperparameters and the dropout are fitted by maximum likelihood on mini-batches of cells. The bulk model (equations 3–5, pp. 6–7) is

\theta_{gj}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\hat\alpha_{gj},\hat\beta_{gj}), \qquad y_{gi}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}\Bigl(K_i\sum_jp_{ji}\theta_{gj}\Bigr), \qquad \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol{N}), \tag{15}

or y_{gi}\sim\mathrm{NB}\bigl(K_i\sum_jp_{ji}r_{gj},P_g\bigr) with r_{gj} and P_g drawn from their fitted priors. K_i is “proportional to the number of cells sequenced and the sequencing depth of the bulk sample” (p. 6). Five dropout configurations, with or without zero inflation of the bulk, are offered (Table S1, p. 14); the bulk dropout, when kept, is d_g=\sum_jp_{ji}d_{gj} (equation 6, p. 7). Only the Dirichlet concentration \boldsymbol{N} is fitted on the bulk; the reference hyperparameters stay fixed (p. 7). Both stages run in Pyro with Adam, clipped gradients and learning-rate decay (pp. 7–8). The 95% intervals of Fig. 3 (p. 11) are read from \mathrm{Dir}(\hat{\boldsymbol{N}}), “the distribution for bulk cell type proportions” (p. 7). The paper describes that fit as gradient steps on the log-likelihood under draws from the Dirichlet and states no variational objective, so the calibration of these intervals cannot be judged from the text (our remark). Genes are independent, and no covariance is modelled.

Aggregation, and when it is exact. The Poisson bulk rests on “the sum of two (or more) Poisson random variables has also a Poisson distribution” (p. 6). If a bulk holds m_{ji} cells of type j whose counts of gene g are independent \mathrm{Poisson}(\theta_{gj}), the total is \mathrm{Poisson}(\sum_jm_{ji}\theta_{gj}), which is Eq. 15 with K_i\propto n_i: an exact convolution of univariate Poissons. The negative-binomial bulk is exact only because P_g is shared by all types: a sum of independent \mathrm{NB}(r_c,P) variables is \mathrm{NB}(\sum_cr_c,P), so m_{ji} cells of type j add up to \mathrm{NB}(\sum_jm_{ji}r_{gj},P_g). With a type-specific P_{gj} the sum is no longer negative binomial, and its law is a finite convolution of the kind DeMixNB evaluates (Sec. 5) (our remark). In the Poisson variant, \theta_{gj} is drawn once per bulk, so every cell of a type shares one rate: the Gamma layer is a random population profile, and \operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})=K_i\sum_jp_{ji}\mathbb{E}\theta_{gj}+K_i^{2}\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\operatorname{Var}\theta_{gj} adds a term quadratic in p_{ji} to the Poisson term, gene by gene (our reading).

Relation to deMixSC, DeMixNB and DeCovarT. deMixSC writes the bulk the same way, as a sum over the cells of each type (supplementary note, equations S.1–S.2, pp. 1–2; Eq. 10), but adds a mean-zero bulk noise with no law and fits weighted NNLS: it uses the sum for the mean only, and it is not a negative-binomial convolution. DeMixNB is the exact convolution of two negative binomials with their own dispersions (Montierth et al. 2025). DeCovarT convolves Gaussian population profiles and keeps their gene–gene covariance. In that order the variance model grows from a weight (deMixSC, rung 2) to a count law per gene (DeconV, DeMixNB, rung 3) to a dense covariance (DeCovarT, rung 5).

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 3, a Poisson or negative-binomial GLM per gene, with a random Gamma rate or log-normal size; response error only, the reference law is plugged in through its fitted hyperparameters; interval from the fitted Dirichlet.

ReDeconv

ReDeconv names three ways a single-cell reference distorts deconvolution: rescaling every cell to a common total (CP10K), which erases transcriptome size; the gene-length mismatch between UMI single-cell counts and full-length bulk libraries; and ignoring the within-type variance (Lu et al. 2025).

Model. The bulk is a sum of m_{ji} independent cells of each type. By the central limit theorem, after a rescaling of the bulk by a constant c and with weights f_{ji}=cm_{ji},

y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\Bigl(\sum_jf_{ji}\tilde\mu_{gj},\ c\sum_jf_{ji}\sigma^{2}_{gj}\Bigr), \tag{16}

with genes independent, and the composition is estimated by maximising the product of these densities over genes. The variance is linear in the weights, the diagonal of the within-type layer n_i^{-1}\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} (one replicate), as in RNA-Sieve without the spread of type means. The optimiser, the estimation of c and the final simplex step are not stated.

Transcriptome size. CLTS normalisation fits, for each single-cell sample r, a line S_{jr}=\alpha_rS_{j1}+\beta_r between its mean transcriptome sizes per type and those of a baseline sample, then rescales every count of sample r as x_{gc}\leftarrow x_{gc}/\alpha_r+(v_{\max}-\beta_r/\alpha_r)/G with v_{\max}=\max_r\beta_r/\alpha_r. Differences of transcriptome size between types within a sample are kept; differences between samples are removed. CLTS therefore keeps S_j in \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}=S_j\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}, so the fitted weights are cell fractions rather than transcript fractions.

Caveats. About 100 signature genes per type are chosen by a t-test against every other type (P<0.05, no multiplicity correction), a fold change of at least 2 and the smallest coefficient of variation (feature-selection review); the synthetic benchmarks draw bulk and reference from the same single-cell source, as the authors acknowledge.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 4; response error only, with a central-limit law over cells; the reference is plugged in.

Multivariate methods: gene–gene covariance

DECALS makes no distributional assumption on the bulk. Its model (equations 1–2, 5) is

\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}_i =\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, \tag{17}

with subject-level type profiles \boldsymbol{x}^{(j)}_i independent across types: exactly the quadratic layer \boldsymbol{S}_B(\boldsymbol{p}) and the purified-profile covariance, without a density. The three panels of ?@fig-dag-decals are the paper’s three estimators.

  1. Constrained OLS (equation 3) is the point estimator. For a large number of genes the inequality constraints are inactive and the estimator is the equality-constrained projection \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=\mathbf{U}\tilde{\boldsymbol{p}} of the OLS solution (Lemma S1). Its asymptotic covariance is the sandwich \boldsymbol{\Xi}_i=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{U}^{\top} with \mathbf{D}=(\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu})^{-1}\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\boldsymbol{\mu}(\tfrac1G\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu})^{-1}.
  2. Constrained GLS with known \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i (equations 10–11) is more efficient. The authors reject it once \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i is estimated: the per-sample inverse square root is too noisy, and the coverage of GLS with an estimated covariance falls to about 0.65–0.8 in their simulations.
  3. Unknown \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j. Because \mathbb{E}[z_{gi}z_{hi}]=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\Sigma_{j,gh}, the residual outer products are regressed on the squared proportions across the N samples, \hat{\boldsymbol{c}}_{gh}=(\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{H}})^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{H}}^{\top}(\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_g\circ\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}_h) with \hat{\mathbf{H}}=[\hat p_{ji}^{2}] (equation 6), a regression first proposed for known proportions by CSNet. Replacing \mathbf{H} by \hat{\mathbf{H}} deflates the estimate; Proposition 1 gives the bias terms \mathbf{B}_1,\mathbf{B}_2 under a Gaussian approximation of \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}, and the corrected estimator (equation 7) is iterated with \boldsymbol{\Xi}_i, then thresholded by SCAD and projected onto the positive semidefinite cone.

Asymptotics. Genes are the statistical units: Theorem 1 gives \sqrt{G}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\to\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{\Xi}_i) as G\to\infty for one sample, under sub-exponential errors, a dependency graph of bounded degree among genes, and p_{ji}>0 for all types. On a face of the simplex the limit law is not derived. With dense gene correlation the authors report that coverage collapses to about 0.65: the central limit theorem over genes fails when dependence is not sparse. The paper gives no consistency theorem for \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 6 for the estimate and its interval, with rung 5 as the efficient variant set aside; response error only, with the composition-dependent covariance of DeCovarT; an asymptotic law over genes yields the sandwich interval.

MEAD is the multivariate errors-in-variables method. Its successive models (?@fig-dag-mead), translated into our indices, are:

  • Scales (equations 2–3). The bulk is \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=a_i\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}^{\mathrm{bulk}})\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_i and reference individual r is \mathbf{Z}_r=a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{b}^{\mathrm{ref}})\mathbf{X}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r+\mathbf{E}_r, with \mathbf{X}_i and \mathbf{X}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r drawn from one population law (assumption 1). a_i captures depth and tissue amount, \boldsymbol{b} gene length and GC content. The reference scale is one scalar per reference individual, shared by its cell types (Supplementary S2.1); the authors avoid per-cell library-size normalisation to keep cell size in \boldsymbol{\mu}.

  • Reparametrisation (equations 4–5). Only the ratio \tilde b_g=b^{\mathrm{bulk}}_g/b^{\mathrm{ref}}_g is identified, and assumption 3 treats it as noise, \tilde b_g\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}[1,\sigma_0^{2}], independent of \boldsymbol{\mu}. The model becomes \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\beta}_i+\boldsymbol{e}_i with \boldsymbol{\beta}_i=a_i\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and \boldsymbol{e}_i=(\tilde{\boldsymbol{B}}-\mathbf{I})\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\beta}_i+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'_i: the platform ratio is not estimated, inflates the variance and makes \boldsymbol{e}_i dependent across samples.

  • One sample. With \hat a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r=\sum_{j,g}z_{rgj}/(JG) (a plug-in from the reference alone), \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot} the average of \boldsymbol{z}_{rg\cdot}/\hat a^{\mathrm{ref}}_r and \hat{\mathbf{K}}_g its covariance across reference individuals, the bias-corrected estimating equation

    \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\hat{\mathbf{K}}\bigr)\boldsymbol{\beta}_i=\boldsymbol{0}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{K}}=\sum_gw_g\hat{\mathbf{K}}_g, \tag{18}

    removes the attenuation caused by a noisy regressor (equation 6). Non-negativity is imposed by truncation or constrained optimisation, and \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i/\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_i\|_1.

  • Several samples (section 5). The composition is regressed on covariates, \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}]=h(\boldsymbol{b}_0+\mathbf{A}_0^{\top}\boldsymbol{f}_i), with \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i} plugged into an estimating equation (11).

  • Dependence and weights. Gene–gene dependence is global, not type specific: a dependency graph over genes, estimated from the bulk correlation by a multiple test, enters only the sandwich covariance. The weights w_g=1/\tilde s_g^{2}, with s_g^{2}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{K}}_g\mathbf{1} shrunk across genes, come from the reference only; MuSiC’s residual-based weights “can severely bias” the estimating equation.

Identifiability (Theorem 1). With a composition matrix of rank J, the proportions are identifiable if and only if \boldsymbol{\mu} has full rank and, for every partition of the genes into t\ge2 blocks, the ranks of the blocks of \boldsymbol{\mu} add to more than J. Perfect marker genes violate the condition: rescaling the platform ratios of the type-j markers by 1/\delta_j, the proportions to \tilde p_{ji}=\delta_jp_{ji}/\sum_\ell\delta_\ell p_{\ell i} and the scale to a_i\sum_\ell\delta_\ell p_{\ell i} leaves the bulk mean unchanged, for any \boldsymbol{\delta}. A gene-wise platform ratio can then mimic a type-specific size factor (Supplementary Remark S1), the \boldsymbol{q} versus \boldsymbol{p} ambiguity of alignment scales; assumption 3 restores identification because a ratio that depends on the type of its marker is no longer independent of \boldsymbol{\mu} (our reading).

Asymptotics. With G\to\infty and the number of reference individuals fixed, Theorems 2–3 give \sqrt{G}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\to\mathcal{N}\bigl(\boldsymbol{0},\nabla g\,\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\boldsymbol{\Upsilon}^{-1}\nabla g^{\top}\bigr), with the Gram limit \boldsymbol{\Upsilon}=\lim G^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\mu}, when every p_{ji}>0 and the dependency graph is “almost sparse”. The regime is fragile when the reference-noise term does not shrink (fixed number of reference individuals), when types are collinear, at the boundary (the softplus device is inconsistent for finite tuning), and for the composition regression unless N=o(G) (Theorem 4, Remark S3). DECALS reports that MEAD underestimates variances.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 2 weights inside a rung 6 estimating equation; both layers, the regressor error removed by a bias-corrected estimating equation and the platform ratio a multiplicative response error; the law is asymptotic in G.

Where DeCovarT sits

The purified-profile fit plugs in the mean and gene–gene covariance of each type and fits the Gaussian convolution of Eq. 20, one bulk sample at a time: rung 5 of Table 3, with a covariance that depends on \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and a full Gaussian likelihood. Against the methods above:

  • RNA-Sieve and ReDeconv sum independent cells, so a type’s variance enters linearly in p_{ji}, gene by gene; DeCovarT convolves random population profiles, so it enters quadratically and keeps the gene–gene covariance.
  • DECALS assumes the same covariance, \sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, without a density; its point estimate is least squares and its efficiency depends on how well the covariance is estimated across bulks. MEAD keeps a global gene dependence and adds the platform ratio, but models the reference noise that DeCovarT ignores.
  • RCTD is a read-level mixture with gene-wise random effects (rung 7), not a type-level covariance.

For a single-cell reference the bulk is a physical sum of cells, and the variance becomes linear in p_{ji}, as in RNA-Sieve: rung 4 with a dense covariance. The strategies that rebuild DeCovarT for that reference, and the three-layer law that combines within- and between-donor covariances, are in the single-cell generative vignette; the model retained for real data is in the MLE vignette.

Cell-type-specific moments when the composition is known

The methods of Sec. 2 estimate the composition from known reference moments. The reverse problem takes the composition \{\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\} as known, from any of those methods, and estimates what DeCovarT plugs in: type-level means and covariances, or the purified profile of each type in each sample. Write the convolution with explicit latent profiles,

\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}\sim(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)\ \text{independent across }j, \qquad \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}=\sum_jp_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i}, \tag{19}

so that

\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}]=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i})=\sum_jp_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j , \tag{20}

which is the purified-profile law when the profiles are Gaussian. Four families use these identities.

  • Type-level gene networks across a cohort. CSNet regresses the outer products of bulk residuals on the squared proportions to estimate each \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, then thresholds the correlation (Sec. 3.1).
  • Sample-level profiles with a covariance across cell types. Unico (Sec. 3.2), and the Bayesian bMIND and EPIC-unmix (Sec. 4.1), place a J\times J covariance \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g across cell types for each gene, independent across genes. Their covariance is the transpose of DeCovarT’s: it couples types within a gene, not genes within a type.
  • Sample-level profiles with a gene–gene covariance. With Gaussian profiles and known moments, the posterior mean of each \boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j,i} is a Wiener filter, which is also the best linear unbiased predictor of the random effects when Eq. 20 is read as a linear mixed model; both are derived in the Wiener-filter vignette.
  • Subject-level references from repeated bulks. imply predicts a profile per subject, shared by that subject’s repeated samples, with a gene-wise linear mixed model, then re-estimates the proportions with it (Sec. 3.3).

On the measurement side, these methods need the bulk on a linear scale (FPKM for CSNet). When the bulk is normalised by its own library size, the known weights act as RNA fractions \boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}, not as cell fractions (Sec. 1).

Type-level moments given known proportions

CSNet inverts the DeCovarT arrow (Su et al. 2024). DeCovarT takes (\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}) as plug-in and returns \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}. CSNet takes \{\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\}_{i=1}^{N} as known (from CIBERSORT, MuSiC, or DeCovarT itself) and returns type-level means and a sparse correlation network. The generative identities are the same convolution as Eq. 19 and Eq. 20, written across a cohort rather than one sample:

\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}] = \sum_j p_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}) = \sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j. \tag{21}

No Gaussian law is required for the moments. Let P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J} have entries P_{ij}=p_{ji} and H\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times J} have entries H_{ij}=p_{ji}^{2}. Gene-wise ordinary least squares on the linear mean recovers

\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot} = (P^{\top}P)^{-1}P^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}_{g\cdot}, \tag{22}

the bulk analogue of a reference average, now identified from compositional contrast across samples rather than from purified cells. Centred residuals z_{gi}=y_{gi}-\sum_j p_{ji}\hat{\mu}_{gj} then satisfy the pairwise identity z_{gi}z_{g'i}=\sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\Sigma_{gg',j}+\varepsilon_{gg'i}. Least squares of the Hadamard products on H estimates each covariance entry,

\hat{\Sigma}_{gg',j} = \bigl[(H^{\top}H)^{-1}H^{\top}(\boldsymbol{z}_{g\cdot}\odot\boldsymbol{z}_{g'\cdot})\bigr]_{j}. \tag{23}

CSNet converts \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j to a correlation \hat{R}_j and applies an element-wise SCAD threshold. That is a marginal co-expression graph, not a Gaussian Markov precision. The Gaussian convolution log-likelihood in \{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}, which is the natural DeCovarT loss for the same parameters, is neither convex nor biconvex in those matrices; pairwise least squares is how CSNet avoids that optimisation (Su et al. 2024).

A DeCovarT-native sequel would keep Eq. 22–Eq. 23 as the moment step and map \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j to a sparse precision \boldsymbol{\Omega}_j (network inference), run after \boldsymbol{p} has been estimated (?@fig-csnet-two-arrows). A CSNet correlation graph is not a DeCovarT precision.

P and H must have full column rank, so \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} has to vary across the N bulks. One sample identifies \boldsymbol{p} given (\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\}); it does not identify J covariance matrices. Rare types with almost constant p_{ji} leave the corresponding column of H weak, which is why CSNet recovers abundant-type co-expression more easily than microglia-scale weights. The method is a moment estimator: modest errors in the supplied \boldsymbol{p} are averaged over N, whereas DeCovarT’s likelihood for a single column is concentrated in \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}.
