Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): the reverse problem, with the composition known and the latent profiles’ moments as the target; rung 1 regressions for both moments.

Sample-level profiles with a covariance across cell types

Unico (Chen et al. 2025) takes the proportions as given, estimated beforehand by a reference-based method, and estimates for each gene the moments of the latent sample-level profiles, then the profiles themselves (a samples \times genes \times types tensor). Its model (equations 3–6, p. 11), in our notation, makes no distributional assumption:

y_{gi}=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}+e_{gi}, \qquad \mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}, \quad \operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g, \qquad \mathbb{E}\,e_{gi}=0, \quad \operatorname{Var}e_{gi}=\tau_g^{2}, \tag{24}

so that \operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2}.

  • Estimator: the model moments of each bulk sample. Each bulk sample has its own law, set by its proportions \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} and the gene parameters \theta_g=\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot},\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g,\tau_g^{2}\}. Unico therefore does not pool the samples into one empirical moment: each sample contributes one condition per moment, which matches a model moment with that sample’s observation and has mean zero under the model (equations 9–11, p. 13),

    f_{1i}(\theta_g)=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}-y_{gi}, \qquad f_{2i}(\theta_g)=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2}-\bigl(y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}\bigr)^{2}. \tag{25}

    The N conditions per moment outnumber the J+J(J+1)/2+1 parameters, so the estimate minimises \boldsymbol{f}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{U}}\boldsymbol{f}, with \hat{\boldsymbol{U}} the inverse covariance of the conditions (equation 12, pp. 13–14) (Hansen 1982). Independent samples make \hat{\boldsymbol{U}} diagonal and the problem weighted least squares; in practice \hat{\boldsymbol{U}} only down-weights samples with large condition values (p. 14).

  • Implementation (p. 14). The means are fitted under non-negativity by the constrained least-squares solver pcls of mgcv; the variances and covariances by COBYLA (nloptr), with a small L_2 penalty against the collinearity of the proportions. Samples more than two standard deviations from the gene mean are dropped. The weights are updated after each iteration: two iterations for the means, three for the (co)variances.

  • What the moments are taken from. The inputs are the bulk matrix and proportions estimated beforehand (p. 11); Unico needs no single-cell reference. Single cells enter the paper only to build benchmark pseudo-bulks: the type-level pseudo-bulk profiles of one randomly drawn donor are mixed with the proportions of another randomly drawn donor (p. 17), so that the true sample-level profiles are known. Bisque’s unpaired mode (Sec. 2.5.6.1) is different: it matches the mean and variance of each gene across bulk samples with those of single-cell pseudo-bulks, two empirical laws. Unico matches the model moments of each bulk sample with that sample’s observation.

  • Profiles. The conditional expectation under a Gaussian working law (Theorem 1, p. 12), \hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{g\cdot,i}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}+\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}(y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot})/(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2}), the gene-wise, J\times J analogue of DeCovarT’s Wiener filter; TCA is the case \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g=\mathbf{I}. Distribution-free asymptotic tests of covariate effects at the cell-type level are offered (Fig. 3b, p. 8).

Critical remarks. \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g is identified only from many bulk samples of varying composition, and the plugged-in proportions are treated as exact. The bulk variance \boldsymbol{p}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p} is quadratic in \boldsymbol{p}, like DeCovarT’s: with \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g=\operatorname{diag}\{(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)_{gg}\}_j it is the variance of gene g under DeCovarT. The off-diagonal of \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g is what DeCovarT drops by assuming independent types; the gene–gene couplings are what Unico drops (our remark).

A confounding between \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g and \tau_g^{2} (our remark). Because \mathbf{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}=1, \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g+c\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top})\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+c for every sample. Adding c to every entry of \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g and subtracting c from \tau_g^{2} leaves every condition of Eq. 25 unchanged, so the bulk moments identify the constant part of \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g and \tau_g^{2} only together, within the range allowed by \tau_g^{2}\ge0 and \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g+c\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\succeq0. The L_2 penalty picks one point of that range. The choice is not neutral downstream. In Theorem 1 the denominator is unchanged, but the numerator gains c\mathbf{1}, so every type’s profile in sample i moves by the same amount c\,(y_{gi}-\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot})/(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\tau_g^{2}), and the cross-type correlations of \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g change with c.

Entropy as a stratifier. Unico summarises \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g by the von Neumann entropy of the J\times J cross-type correlation: the entropy of its normalised eigenvalues, scaled to [0,1] (pp. 19–20). The entropy only splits genes at the median for evaluation; it does not filter them. Low-entropy genes, with strong cross-type correlation, gain most from modelling \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g (average correlation improvement 20.0% against 14.9%, p. 6). By the remark above, the entropy of an estimated \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g inherits the c\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} shift (our remark). The analogue for DeCovarT’s G\times G covariance is in the feature-selection vignette.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): the reverse problem again, rung 4, with a variance quadratic in \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i} through a J\times J covariance across types, and two-moment conditions per bulk sample solved by a generalised method of moments; the proportions are plugged in as exact.

Subject-specific references from repeated bulks (imply) 

%%| label: fig-dag-imply
%%| fig-cap: Stage II of `imply` [@mengImplyImprovingCelltype2024] in this vignette's notation. Subjects $n$ are the independent units; their $t_n$ repeated bulk samples $i$ are correlated replicates. For gene $g$ and type $j$, the subject reference $r_{gjn}$ is a fixed group mean plus a subject random effect; the bulk mean mixes the subject references with the stage-I proportions $\hat\theta_{j,ni}$, held fixed. Stage III re-estimates the proportions by non-negative least squares with $\boldsymbol{R}_n=[r_{gjn}]$.

imply estimates a reference per subject from that subject’s repeated bulk samples, then deconvolves those samples again with it (Meng et al. 2024). It assumes that the repeated samples of one subject, for example several brain regions or longitudinal draws, share one cell-type-specific profile and differ only in composition (p. 4). Single cells, or cell lines, enter only through the population signature of stage I. Below, n is the subject, i one of its t_n repeated samples, j the type and g the gene (the paper uses k for the type).

  1. Stage I (p. 4). \nu-support vector regression of each sample on a population signature; negative estimates are set to zero and the rest renormalised, which gives \hat\theta_{j,ni}.

  2. Stage II (pp. 4–5). For each gene, a linear mixed model with the stage-I proportions as covariates,

    \mathbb{E}(y_{g,ni})=\sum_j\bigl(m_{gj}+\beta_{gj}z_n+u_{gjn}\bigr)\hat\theta_{j,ni}, \tag{26}

    with z_n a binary group label, fixed effects m_{gj} (control mean) and \beta_{gj} (group difference), and a subject random effect u_{gjn}. It is fitted by penalised least squares with restricted maximum likelihood (REML), and the subject reference is r_{gjn}=\hat m_{gj}+z_n\hat\beta_{gj}+\hat u_{gjn} (p. 5): the best linear unbiased predictor of the subject’s profile. The covariance of u_{gjn} across types is not stated in the main text.

  3. Stage III (p. 5). Non-negative least squares jointly over the samples of subject n, \min_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}_n\ge0}\lVert(\boldsymbol{R}_n\otimes\mathbf{I}_{t_n})\operatorname{vec}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_n^{\top})-\operatorname{vec}(\boldsymbol{y}_n^{\top})\rVert_2, by quadratic programming.

Reading. Stage II is the reverse problem of Sec. 3 at the subject level: the composition is known, the profiles are random, and the BLUP returns them. It is the gene-wise analogue of DeCovarT’s Wiener filter read as a linear mixed model (LMM reading), with one random effect shared by the t_n repeated samples of a subject instead of one profile per bulk sample, and no gene–gene covariance. The stage-III objective equals \sum_i\lVert\boldsymbol{R}_n\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot ni}-\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot ni}\rVert^{2} under element-wise non-negativity, so the joint fit separates into one NNLS per sample with a shared \boldsymbol{R}_n (our remark). The same samples build \boldsymbol{R}_n and are deconvolved with it, and the stage-I proportions enter stage II as exact covariates: the data are used twice, and no interval is returned (our remark).

Perspective: a count mixed model (ours). The linear mixed model is the Gaussian member of rung 7. On counts, the natural extension is a negative-binomial mixed model with an identity link on the mixture mean, \mathbb{E}(y_{g,ni}\mid u)=s_{ni}\sum_j(m_{gj}+\beta_{gj}z_n+u_{gjn})\hat\theta_{j,ni} and \operatorname{Var}(y_{g,ni}\mid u)=\mathbb{E}+\mathbb{E}^{2}/\phi_g, with s_{ni} a library size, fitted by Laplace approximation as in glmmTMB-type software. TODO-cite: Brooks et al. 2017, glmmTMB balances speed and flexibility among packages for zero-inflated generalized linear mixed modeling, The R Journal 9(2):378-400, doi:10.32614/RJ-2017-066; not in inst/REFERENCES.bib or inst/packages.bib. The identity link keeps the physical sum of cells; a log link would mix logarithms (caveat 1 of Sec. 7). The mean must then stay positive, a constraint the solver has to enforce.

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 7 for the subject references (a Gaussian linear mixed model), rung 1 for the final proportions (NNLS with \boldsymbol{R}_n plugged in); the stage-I proportions are treated as exact; no interval.

Bayesian reference-based deconvolution

Bayesian methods put priors on the purified profiles, on the proportions, or on both, and report posterior summaries. They split by target: sample-level profiles (Sec. 4.1) or proportions (Sec. 4.2). A latent-profile Bayesian version of DeCovarT is derived in the Bayesian Wiener-filter vignette.

Cell-type-specific profiles 

%%| label: fig-dag-bayes-cts
%%| fig-cap: Bayesian models for cell-type-specific profiles, in this review's notation. (a) `bMIND` and `EPIC-unmix`: for each gene, the sample-level profile across cell types is Gaussian with a $J\times J$ covariance $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g$ under an inverse-Wishart prior centred on single-cell estimates; proportions are fixed. (b) `BLADE`: log-normal profiles with a normal-gamma prior, Dirichlet proportions, linear mixing. (c) `BEDwARS`: a cohort-level signature drawn around a noisy reference, Dirichlet proportions, Gaussian residuals.

bMIND estimates sample-level profiles for proportions estimated beforehand (by NNLS or Bisque) (Wang et al. 2020). For gene g and subject i,

y_{gi}=\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}+e_{gi}, \qquad \boldsymbol{x}_{g\cdot,i}\sim\mathcal{N}_J(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot},\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g), \qquad e_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_g^{2}), \tag{27}

with \boldsymbol{\mu}_{g\cdot}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{g\cdot},0.5\mathbf{I}), \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_g\sim\mathrm{IW}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}_g,50) and a non-informative prior on \sigma_g^{2}; the hyperparameters come from single-cell or single-nucleus summary statistics. Sampling is by MCMC (MCMCglmm), gene by gene. Condition-specific means \boldsymbol{\mu}_g^{f} give tests of cell-type-specific differential expression. The authors note that the uncertainty of the estimated proportions is not propagated.

EPIC-unmix (Tang et al. 2025) keeps the bMIND model and adds a second, empirical-Bayes step: the prior is re-centred on the step-one posterior means and on their covariance across the target samples, with an increased number of degrees of freedom The target samples are therefore used twice. The bulk enters on the \log_2 scale, so the linear mixing of Eq. 27 is a mixing of logarithms, which is not the physical sum of cells (\log\sum_jp_jx_j\neq\sum_jp_j\log x_j).

BLADE estimates proportions and sample-level profiles jointly (Andrade Barbosa et al. 2021): y_{gi}=\sum_jp_{ji}x_{gj,i} plus a log-normal error, with x_{gj,i}\sim\mathrm{LN}(m_{gj},\lambda_{gj}^{-1}), a normal-gamma prior on (m_{gj},\lambda_{gj}) centred on the log-scale mean and variance of single-cell data, and \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_1). The mixing is on the linear scale (TPM). Inference is collapsed variational, with hyperparameters chosen on a grid by likelihood. The model is diagonal: no covariance across genes or across types.

BEDwARS treats the reference itself as noisy (Ghaffari et al. 2023): y_{gi}=\sum_j\mu_{gj}p_{ji}+E_{gi}, \log\mu_{gj}\sim\log\mu^{r}_{gj}+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_j^{2}\log\mu^{r}_{gj}), \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha\boldsymbol{p}_0), with half-Cauchy hyperpriors and Metropolis–Hastings chains. The signature is cohort-level: there is no sample-level profile. As written, the prior variance \sigma_j^{2}\log\mu^{r}_{gj} is not positive for reference values at or below one RPKM (our remark).

BayesPrism places a multinomial likelihood on bulk counts with a patient-derived single-cell prior and infers proportions and sample-level profiles jointly by Gibbs sampling (Chu et al. 2022). The multinomial is the Poisson measurement model conditioned on the library size (Sec. 1.1), so BayesPrism is the count-scale member of this family. When the reference is updated, the non-malignant profiles pooled across bulks deviate from the single-cell profiles by gene-wise fold changes with a weak, zero-mean log-normal prior (\sigma=2, pp. 5–6): a gene-wise random effect that absorbs platform factors, as \gamma_g does in RCTD (our reading). The read model has no overdispersion, and genes are coupled only through the multinomial total.

The contrast with DeCovarT is the dimension of the covariance. bMIND and EPIC-unmix model how cell types covary for one gene across subjects; DeCovarT models how genes covary within one cell type. A separable covariance \operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{vec}\boldsymbol{X}_i)=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\otimes\boldsymbol{\Sigma} for the G\times J matrix of purified profiles would contain both as special cases (our remark); no reviewed method fits it.

BLEND: a per-sample mixture of references 

%%| label: fig-dag-blend
%%| fig-cap: `BLEND` [@huangBLENDProbabilisticCellular2024] in this vignette's notation. Each bulk sample $i$ draws RNA fractions $\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}$ and, for each type $j$, weights $\boldsymbol{\psi}_{j,i}$ over the $M_j$ observed references $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{j,m}$; the sample's reference for type $j$ is their convex combination. Each read draws a type, then a gene from that type's sample reference, so the gene counts are multinomial.

Inside a read plate, a latent type label Y i r drawn from q i and the sample reference of that type generate the observed gene identity X tilde i r, categorical.

BLEND is the count member of this family with several references per type (Huang et al. 2024). Its generative model (p. 8) is latent Dirichlet allocation with per-sample topics. For bulk sample i with read depth R_i,

\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}), \qquad \boldsymbol{\psi}_{j,i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\beta}_j), \qquad \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i},\{\boldsymbol{\psi}_{j,i}\} \sim\mathrm{Mult}\Bigl(R_i,\ \sum_jq_{ji}\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{B}}_{j,i}\Bigr), \qquad \boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{B}}_{j,i}=\sum_{m=1}^{M_j}\psi_{j,i,m}\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{j,m}, \tag{28}

where the \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{j,m} are the observed references of type j, each a distribution over genes. The reference of type j in sample i thus lies in the convex hull of the observed references (p. 8). The multinomial collects the reads of steps (iii)–(v) of the paper, each drawn independently given the fractions and the weights (our rewriting).

  • Inference (pp. 9–10). Gibbs sampling, after each read is given its reference source as an extra latent label, with all entries of \boldsymbol{\alpha} and \boldsymbol{\beta}_j set to 0.01; or EM for the maximum a posteriori estimate under the simplex constraints. On one bulk sample of 6,388 genes with nine references, the Gibbs sampler takes 36 minutes and EM-MAP 1.5 minutes (p. 10). The authors call these priors non-informative; a Dirichlet with concentrations 0.01 favours sparse weights, near the vertices of the simplex (our remark).
  • Cell size (p. 10). \boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i} are RNA fractions; cell fractions are p_{ji}=(q_{ji}/S_j)/\sum_{j'}(q_{j'i}/S_{j'}), with S_j given or estimated by average library sizes.
  • Stated limits (p. 7). “Gene-gene correlation is ignored in BLEND for model simplicity”, and, although the posterior is available, “statistical inference for cellular fractions is not appropriate”.

Comparison with the Wiener filter. Both BLEND and DeCovarT’s latent-profile form (Wiener filter) return a profile per type and per bulk sample. BLEND restricts it to the hull of the observed references: at most M_j-1 free weights per type, on the scale of relative abundances, so a deviation that no reference shows cannot be expressed. The Wiener filter shrinks the bulk residual continuously onto each type along \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, can return any vector in \mathbb{R}^{G}, and has a closed-form posterior covariance (posterior covariance). Gene dependence is not absent from BLEND: across samples, \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{\mathrm{B}}_{j,i})=\boldsymbol{\Phi}_j\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\psi}_{j,i})\boldsymbol{\Phi}_j^{\top}, with \boldsymbol{\Phi}_j=[\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{j,1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{j,M_j}], a gene–gene covariance of rank at most M_j-1 carried by the references (our remark). With a sample covariance of the M_j references plugged in as \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, the Wiener filter would be the Gaussian, continuous counterpart of that hull (our remark).

Ladder and errors in variables (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 2.2): rung 7, a multinomial given latent fractions and reference weights; the reference error is modelled only as a choice within the hull of the observed references; posterior summaries, which the authors do not use for inference.

Proportions

(a) `DSection`: Gaussian bulk on linear intensities with condition-specific type profiles, a gene-wise precision and an informative Dirichlet prior on the proportions. (b) `gnSPADE`: each UMI of a spot draws a type label and then a gene, so the spot counts are multinomial with a probability vector that mixes the type profiles; a gene network enters as a Markov random field on the labels.

DSection is the continuous, Gaussian route (Erkkilä et al. 2010): y_{gi}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\sum_jp_{ji}x_{gjh(i)},\lambda_g^{-1}\bigr), with type profiles specific to the condition h(i) of sample i, x_{gjh}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{gjh},\eta^{2}), \lambda_g\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta) and \boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(w_0\boldsymbol{p}_{0i}) centred on a prior guess of the proportions, which is needed for identifiability. Sampling is Gibbs for the profiles and the precision and Metropolis–Hastings with Dirichlet proposals for the proportions. The paper offers no log-normal option and recommends linear data. The variance depends on the gene but not on the proportions.

gnSPADE (Xie and Cui 2026) is the count route, and it is reference-free. Each UMI of spot i draws a label z\sim\mathrm{Mult}(\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}) and then a gene from the profile of that label, so \boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\mid\boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathrm{Mult}(L_i,\sum_jq_{ji}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\cdot j}), with L_i the number of UMIs: latent Dirichlet allocation with a Markov random field over the labels built from a protein interaction network. Inference is collapsed Gibbs.

The two differ where the measurement model of Sec. 1 bites.

  • Variance. In gnSPADE the variance is fixed by the mean (the multinomial is a Poisson measurement conditioned on the total). In DSection it is a free gene-wise constant that does not grow with the mean, which a UMI measurement contradicts.
  • What the weights are. gnSPADE shares UMIs, so the label probabilities are transcript fractions \boldsymbol{q}_{\cdot i}; converting them to cell fractions needs S_j. DSection estimates whatever its reference scale encodes.
  • Profile variability. Neither model has a type-level variability of profiles across samples beyond the prior of DSection; neither has a gene–gene covariance. The gene network of gnSPADE acts on labels, not on expression.

Semi-reference deconvolution: one unknown component

Semi-reference methods have references for J-1 types and estimate an unknown component, usually tumour, together with the proportions. With one component unknown, the convolution of univariate laws has to be written explicitly, and its tractability drives the choice of law.

%%| label: fig-dag-semiref
%%| fig-cap: Two semi-reference convolutions of univariate components. (a) `DeMixT`: log-normal components mixed linearly on the raw scale; the density of the sum has no closed form and is integrated numerically. (b) `DeMixNB`: each component is a negative binomial whose mean is already scaled by its proportion; the density of the sum is an exact finite sum.
%%| filename: fig-dag-semiref
%%| alt: Two panels, each inside a plate over samples and genes. Panel a: fixed reference parameters generate latent log-normal normal components N_k; fixed unknown-component parameters generate a latent log-normal tumour component T; with fixed proportions pi_i they generate the observed y_gi through a linear mixture whose density is obtained numerically. Panel b: fixed reference and tumour parameters and a fixed proportion pi_i generate two latent negative binomial components N and T; their sum is the observed y_gi, with an exact finite-sum convolution.

\node[ptitle] at (-3.4,1.0) {(b) DeMixNB: negative binomial thinning};
\end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}

DeMix and DeMixT. DeMix mixes a tumour and one normal component; DeMixT adds a second normal component (Ahn et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2018):

y_{gi}=\pi_{1,i}N_{1,gi}+\pi_{2,i}N_{2,gi}+(1-\pi_{1,i}-\pi_{2,i})T_{gi}, \qquad N_{j,gi},T_{gi}\sim\log_2\text{-normal}. \tag{29}

The mixing is linear on the raw scale, and the density of a sum of log-normals has no closed form, so DeMixT integrates numerically (a double integral for three components). The normal-component parameters are plugged in from unmatched normal samples; the proportions and the tumour parameters are maximised by iterated conditional modes, gene and sample blocks in parallel. When the two normal means are close, the likelihood is flat in (\pi_1,\pi_2); a gene-set component-merging step first estimates the tumour proportion on genes where they agree. Genes are independent.

DeMixNB replaces the log-normal by a negative binomial for sparse counts (miRNA, spatial spots) (Montierth et al. 2025): T_{gi}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\pi_i\mu_{tg},\phi_{tg}), N_{gi}\sim\mathrm{NB}((1-\pi_i)\mu_{ng},\phi_{ng}) and y_{gi}=T_{gi}+N_{gi}, whose density is the finite sum \sum_{z=0}^{y}f_T(z)f_N(y-z). The proportions scale the means, not the dispersions. Read with Sec. 1, \mathrm{NB}(\pi\mu,\phi) is the binomial thinning of \mathrm{NB}(\mu,\phi): a Poisson measurement of a Gamma-distributed rate, with the rates mixed linearly (our remark). That makes DeMixNB the semi-reference model closest to a UMI measurement. Its \pi_i is a transcript fraction. The method is a preprint.

BayICE models \log(\text{count}+1) as Gaussian with mean \alpha_g+\sum_jw_{ji}\beta_{gj}+w_{0i}\beta_{g0}, a convex combination of type effects plus an unknown-class effect, with spike-and-slab priors on the type effects (marker selection with a Bayesian false discovery rate) and a Dirichlet prior on the weights (Tai et al. 2021). Inference is Gibbs with Metropolis–Hastings steps. The mixing is on the log scale, so it is a mean regression rather than a convolution, and the variances are gene-wise, not type-specific.

ISOpureR places a multinomial on the discretised tumour profile, with probability vector \alpha_i\boldsymbol{c}_i+\sum_r\omega_{ri}\boldsymbol{x}^{\mathrm{ref}}_r: the normal part is a convex combination of individual reference samples, the cancer profile \boldsymbol{c}_i is shrunk towards a cohort mean by a Dirichlet prior, and the estimate is a MAP by block coordinate descent (Anghel et al. 2015). Genes are coupled through the multinomial simplex; there is no overdispersion. Its \alpha_i is a fraction of transcripts.

Reference-free deconvolution with co-expression structure

Without a reference, deconvolution is a non-negative matrix factorisation \boldsymbol{Y}\approx\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{P} with the columns of \boldsymbol{P} on the simplex. Three recent methods add gene–gene structure to that factorisation, in three different ways.

DSSC (Wang et al. 2024) fits the bulk and, in addition, the Gram matrices of genes and of samples :

\min_{\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{P}\ge 0} \lVert\boldsymbol{Y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{P}\rVert_F^{2} +\lambda_1\lVert\boldsymbol{K}_N-\boldsymbol{P}^{\top}\boldsymbol{P}\rVert_F^{2} +\lambda_2\lVert\boldsymbol{K}_G-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\rVert_F^{2} +\lambda_c\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}-\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{Y}_{\mathrm{sc}})\rVert_F^{2}, \tag{30}

where \boldsymbol{K}_G and \boldsymbol{K}_N are similarity kernels 1/(1+d) built from Pearson distances of the same bulk, and the last term optionally pulls the signature towards a transform \mathcal{T} of a single-cell reference. Multiplicative updates are run without the sum-to-one constraint and the proportions are normalised afterwards. The gene term matches \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top} to a data similarity; expanded, it keeps the affinity part of a graph-Laplacian penalty and replaces its degree term by a quartic term, so it corresponds to no Gaussian Markov random field (our remark).

GSNMF+ (Li et al. 2025) regularises the rows of the signature with a kernel co-expression graph built on the bulk augmented by single-cell pseudo-bulks, and pulls marker rows towards the simplex vertices It states identifiability conditions (separability, or sufficiently scattered factors) and that the Frobenius loss is the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate. With a Euclidean distance its graph term would be \operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{L}_G\boldsymbol{\mu}), the log-density of an intrinsic Gaussian Markov random field prior on the signature; with the cosine distance it uses, the term is quartic.

%%| label: fig-dag-swcam
%%| fig-cap: `swCAM` read as a probabilistic model (our reading, not the paper's). The nuclear-norm penalty on the sample-specific deviations of type $j$ is the MAP of a Gaussian factor model with loadings $\boldsymbol{L}_j$ and sample scores $\boldsymbol{u}_{ij}$, which implies a low-rank gene–gene covariance within each cell type.
%%| filename: fig-dag-swcam
%%| alt: Latent loadings L_j inside a cell-type plate and latent scores u_ij inside a sample plate give the deterministic deviation Delta_i. With the fixed signature mu and fixed proportions p_i, the deviation generates the observed bulk y_i as mu plus Delta_i times p_i plus noise.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[latent] (V) at (2,0.8) {$\boldsymbol{L}_j$};
\node[fixed] (mu) at (4.4,0.8) {$\boldsymbol{\mu}$};
\node[latent] (u) at (0,-2.3) {$\boldsymbol{u}_{ij}$};
\node[det] (D) at (2,-2.3) {$\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i$};
\node[fixed] (p) at (4.4,-2.3) {$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[obs] (y) at (3.2,-4.3) {$\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}$};
\node[note, left=3mm of y] (n1) {$\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{(j)}_i=\boldsymbol{L}_j\boldsymbol{u}_{ij}$};
\node[note, right=3mm of y] (n2) {$(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i)\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i$};
\draw[dependency] (V) -- (D); \draw[dependency] (u) -- (D); \draw[dependency] (D) -- (y);
\draw[dependency] (mu) -- (y); \draw[dependency] (p) -- (y);
\plate{types}{(V)}{$j=1,\ldots,J$}
\plate{samples}{(u)(D)(p)(y)(n1)(n2)}{$i=1,\ldots,N$}
\end{tikzpicture}

swCAM estimates sample-specific signatures (Chen et al. 2022). After convex analysis of mixtures has fixed \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{P}, it solves

\min_{\{\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i\}} \tfrac12\sum_i\lVert\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}-(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i)\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}\rVert_2^{2} +\lambda\sum_j\lVert\boldsymbol{T}_j\rVert_{*}, \tag{31}

where \boldsymbol{T}_j stacks the deviations of type j over samples and \lVert\cdot\rVert_* is the nuclear norm. The problem is convex for fixed \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{P} and is solved by ADMM. There is no co-expression graph. Because \lVert\boldsymbol{T}\rVert_*=\min_{\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{T}}\tfrac12(\lVert\boldsymbol{A}\rVert_F^{2}+\lVert\boldsymbol{B}\rVert_F^{2}), the penalty is the MAP of a Gaussian factor model (?@fig-dag-swcam), which implies a low-rank gene–gene covariance within each type.

Three ways gene covariance enters deconvolution

  1. Graph regularisation of a factorisation. A co-expression graph smooths the signature (GSNMF+). Its probabilistic reading is a Gaussian Markov random field prior on the signature, exact only for a Euclidean, quadratic penalty.
  2. Similarity matching to the bulk itself. The Gram matrices of the factors are fitted to similarities computed from the same data (DSSC). The data are used twice, and no likelihood is implied.
  3. Covariance in a likelihood, a moment equation or a prior. The gene–gene covariance of each type enters the bulk law: as a plug-in in DeCovarT, as moment equations in DECALS and MEAD, as the estimand in CSNet, and implicitly as a low-rank factor structure in swCAM. bMIND and EPIC-unmix belong here with the transposed object, a covariance across cell types.

All three reference-free methods use a squared Frobenius loss, that is a homoscedastic Gaussian likelihood, and therefore ignore the mean–variance relationship of counts (Sec. 1.1).

Synthesis

Caveats and defaults

  1. Scale. Mixing is additive only on a linear scale. Methods that mix logarithms (BayICE, EPIC-unmix) estimate weights of a different, non-physical sum.
  2. Cell versus RNA fractions. Count and topic models (ISOpureR, gnSPADE, DeMixNB, BayesPrism) and any fit on library-normalised bulk return transcript fractions; cell fractions need the cell sizes S_j (RNA-to-cell conversion).
  3. Mean–variance relationship. A residual variance that does not grow with the mean (DSection, BEDwARS, NMF with a Frobenius loss, on rungs 1 and 2) contradicts the Poisson measurement of UMI counts, whose variance grows with the mean. Count likelihoods or explicit variance functions respect it (GLM view).
  4. Linear or quadratic weights. Independent cells give a variance linear in the proportions (RNA-Sieve, ReDeconv); a random population profile gives a quadratic weight (MuSiC, DECALS, CSNet, DeCovarT). Single-cell references with one donor identify only the first (single-cell generative vignette).
  5. Which covariance. G\times G within a type (DeCovarT, DECALS, CSNet) and J\times J within a gene (bMIND, EPIC-unmix, Unico) answer different questions; neither family fits both.
  6. Data reuse. Empirical-Bayes re-centring on the target samples (EPIC-unmix), similarity graphs built from the bulk being factorised (DSSC, GSNMF+) and priors built from the same single-cell source as the benchmark bulk (BLADE group mode) inflate apparent accuracy.
  7. Propagated uncertainty. Weighted moment estimators (MuSiC, SCDC, DWLS, deMixSC) return point estimates only (Sec. 2.3). Few methods propagate the uncertainty of the reference (RNA-Sieve, MEAD, DeCovarT’s reference bootstrap) or of the proportions into downstream profiles (bMIND and Unico do not).
  8. Identifiability. Gene-wise scales with perfect markers (MEAD), collinear reference means (DeMixT), and reference-free factorisations without separability (GSNMF+) all leave the proportions unidentified, whatever the sample size.
